title: Logarithmic-color approximation of 3-colorable graphs
formal:
Is there a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every \(n\)-vertex graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, produces a proper colouring using \(O(\log n)\) colours in expectation? More precisely, do there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and an absolute integer \(K\geq1\) for which
\[
\mathbb E_{\rho}\big[\kappa(A(G;\rho))\big]\leq K\max\{1,\log_2 n\}
\]
for every nonempty \(3\)-colourable graph \(G\), where \(\kappa\) counts distinct colours used? Randomization and expected performance follow the source’s approximation-algorithm convention; deterministic algorithms are included. Properness is always required, and the time bound is worst case as specified below.
why: Logarithmic colouring would be a major improvement for a canonical approximation problem whose positive guarantees still grow as powers of the input size. It would show that a hidden partition into three independent sets can be replaced efficiently by a very small exact partition without needing to recover the original three classes.
status_note: The textbook explicitly poses the logarithmic-colour target as Problem 9. Its randomized approximation convention and colouring chapter support the expected-performance model fixed here. The February 2026 primary paper still gives a power-of-n palette guarantee and records the constant-palette hardness frontier. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 did not identify a resolution of the logarithmic target; this source-open assessment is dated evidence rather than an exhaustive proof of present openness.

progress.text: Williamson and Shmoys identify logarithmic-colour approximation of three-colourable graphs as Problem 9, following their treatment of combinatorial and randomized SDP algorithms.
The algebraic PCSP framework establishes hardness at five colours; it does not provide a logarithmic-palette lower bound.
Bansal, Huang and Lee report an improved polynomial-time growing-palette algorithm with exponent 0.19539.

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation challenge seeking a qualitative improvement from polynomially growing to logarithmic palettes under the simplest nontrivial colouring promise.
importance.basis: Individual review of the exact textbook Problem 9, randomized approximation convention, full logarithmic quantifiers, fixed-palette hardness and the February 2026 algorithmic bound.

sentences: Every promised input graph admits a proper colouring with three colours, but that hidden colouring is not given.
The question asks for a uniform polynomial-time algorithm using only logarithmically many colours in expectation.
Randomness follows the source’s approximation convention while every produced colouring must be exactly proper.
Recent growing-palette algorithms and fixed-palette hardness results leave this logarithmic guarantee unestablished.
An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility of the full algorithmic guarantee in Lean.

definitions:
The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An explicit unary size header is followed by its adjacency matrix, so the input length \(L\) includes isolated vertices and is of order \(n^2+1\). There are no loops or parallel edges and no restriction on degree, connectedness, density or induced subgraphs. The promise says only that some proper colouring with at most three colours exists. The colouring is not supplied, and the input need not be randomly generated.

A proper colouring is an explicit vector \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\) with \(c_i\in[n]\) and \(c_i\ne c_j\) whenever \(\{i,j\}\in E\). Its palette size is \(\kappa(c)=|\{c_i:i\in[n]\}|\). Colour names can be relabeled without changing \(\kappa\). Output the colour indices in vertex order in binary with delimiters. On the empty graph, the algorithm outputs the empty colouring with palette size zero. The logarithm in the bound has base two; changing its base only changes the absolute constant. Using \(\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\) fixes the cases \(n=1,2\) without imposing an asymptotic exception.

Use a uniform randomized multitape Turing machine. There are fixed integers \(C,d\geq1\) bounding the number of bit operations by \(C(L+1)^d\) on every graph and every random-bit sequence. Independent fair bits are the only random resource, so there are polynomially many random bits per run. There is no advice, oracle, exact-real arithmetic or free infinite-precision sampling. All numerical approximations, verification and output writing count toward time. The program, \(K,C,d\) are independent of \(n\) and \(G\).

The algorithm must output a proper colouring on every valid graph and every random-bit sequence; the palette-size guarantee applies only to the promised \(3\)-colourable graphs. Requiring universal properness introduces no new approximation obstruction: a candidate colouring can be checked in polynomial time, and any failure can be replaced by the trivial colouring assigning a different colour to each vertex. On malformed graph encodings the algorithm may reject in polynomial time. The expectation is over the internal random bits for each fixed promised graph, not over an input distribution.

The asymptotic existential target is equivalent to allowing a polynomial-time randomized algorithm to return a proper \(K'\max\{1,\log_2 n\}\)-colouring with probability at least \(2/3\) for every promised graph, for some absolute \(K'\). An expected bound implies this by Markov’s inequality after multiplying its constant by three. Conversely, a bounded-error algorithm can be run independently \(O(\log n)\) times, retaining a verified small colouring if one appears and otherwise using the \(n\)-colour fallback. Reducing failure probability to at most \(1/n\) makes the expected number of colours at most the successful palette bound plus one. The constant and running-time exponent remain fixed. This equivalence does not require derandomization and does not permit a small fraction of incorrectly coloured edges.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and absolute constants exist, or a proof in Lean that no algorithm in the stated class exists. A positive proof must cover every promised graph, always return a proper colouring, account for worst-case bit complexity and prove the expected logarithmic palette bound with one constant \(K\). The equivalent bounded-error formulation may be used if its conversion to the stated guarantee is proved.

A negative proof must rule out every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm and every absolute logarithmic-bound constant, rather than only a particular SDP relaxation, local procedure or deterministic subclass. Hardness conditional on an unproved assumption is partial progress on this unconditional target. A bound \(O(n^\alpha)\) for fixed \(\alpha>0\), a bound \(O((\log n)^c)\) for \(c>1\), a colouring of only part of the vertices, or a guarantee for random or structurally restricted graphs does not meet the required logarithmic bound. This is an algorithm-existence question, so there is no replacement of the asymptotic palette guarantee by an additive numerical tolerance.

source_formulation.text: Find a polynomial-time algorithm that uses only logarithmically many colours on every graph known to be three-colourable.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 9. Randomized expected performance is made explicit using the book’s Chapter 5 convention and the randomized colouring context of §13.2; a separate derandomization requirement is not added.

context_blocks.text: The promise guarantees a partition into three independent sets but does not reveal any of them. Finding that exact partition is computationally hard. The question allows a growing palette, asking whether that relaxation is enough to reduce the output from a power of the graph size to a logarithm.

A standard way to build a colouring is to repeatedly remove a large independent set and assign it a fresh colour. Every induced subgraph of a three-colourable graph is still three-colourable. If one could efficiently find an independent set containing a fixed positive fraction of the remaining vertices at every stage, the number of stages would be logarithmic. This is a useful sufficient route, not an asserted equivalence between logarithmic colouring and a particular independent-set approximation.

The textbook develops Wigderson’s combinatorial ideas and semidefinite relaxations with randomized rounding. Its §13.2 analyses the expected size of independent sets produced by such rounding, and Problem 9 isolates the \(O(\log n)\) palette goal. Making randomization explicit preserves this surrounding algorithmic context; it does not demand that an eventual solution also be derandomized.

The February 2026 theorem of Bansal, Huang and Lee reports \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours, improving the previously stated growing-palette bounds. Its analysis combines combinatorial progress in dense graphs with semidefinite methods in sparse graphs and uses deeper neighborhoods in the rounding argument. For any fixed positive exponent, a power of \(n\) eventually exceeds every constant multiple of \(\log n\), so that improvement leaves the target’s asymptotic form unchanged.

The unconditional three-versus-five hardness theorem concerns a fixed output palette. A logarithmic palette eventually has more than five colours, so that theorem does not rule it out. Conversely, a logarithmic colouring algorithm would not give any fixed constant palette. The constant-colour and logarithmic-colour questions therefore remain distinct despite sharing the same input promise.

Properness is an exact combinatorial condition that can be checked directly. The uncertainty in the randomized formulation concerns the number of colours and is averaged over the algorithm’s coins for each input. A procedure that succeeds only on typical random graphs or leaves a few monochromatic edges would change the mathematical task.
